title: Pearl Harbor: The Warnings Nobody Heeded
alt_titles: Pearl Harbor, Minute by Minute: 7 December 1941
How Pearl Harbor Happened, and What Japan Missed
Pearl Harbor: The Attack That Brought America Into WWII
thumbnail_file: USS Arizona (BB-39) burning at Pearl Harbor 1941.jpg
description_summary: At 7.02am on 7 December 1941, a radar station in Hawaii picked up a huge formation of aircraft. Less than an hour later, Japan attacked Pearl Harbor. This is the story of the warnings, the attack, what Japan missed, and how it brought the United States into the Second World War.

scenes.narration: It was just after seven on the morning of Sunday the seventh of December 1941. At a radar station in Hawaii, two young American soldiers saw something strange. A huge echo was heading for the island of Oahu from the north, more than a hundred and thirty miles out. They phoned it in. They were told not to worry.

The officer on duty, Lieutenant Kermit Tyler, was on his second day of training. A flight of American bombers was due in from California that morning, and he assumed this was them. The radar operators had not told him how big the echo was. It was not. It was the first wave of more than one hundred and eighty Japanese aircraft.

shots.caption: The Opana radar plot of the incoming planes

card.label: Japanese planes in the first wave

scenes.narration: Less than an hour later, they struck the United States Pacific Fleet at Pearl Harbor. By the end of the morning, more than two thousand four hundred Americans were dead. This is the story of that attack, and how it pulled the United States into the Second World War.

shots.file: File:USS Arizona (BB-39) burning at Pearl Harbor 1941.jpg
shots.caption: USS Arizona burning, 7 December 1941
Smoke over Pearl Harbor during the attack

scenes.narration: By 1941, Japan had been at war in China for four years. In 1940 and 1941, its troops also moved into French Indochina. The United States responded with economic pressure. In the summer of 1941, it stopped exporting oil to Japan.

shots.caption: Japanese troops in French Indochina, 1941

card.text: The United States stops oil exports to Japan

scenes.narration: Japan imported most of its oil, and much of it had come from America. Without new supplies, its navy would eventually run dry. Japan's leaders decided to seize the oil-rich lands of South-East Asia, including the Dutch East Indies. That meant war with Britain, the Netherlands and almost certainly the United States.

shots.caption: An oil refinery in the Dutch East Indies

scenes.narration: To stop the American fleet in Hawaii from interfering, Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto planned a surprise attack on Pearl Harbor. Yamamoto had studied in the United States and knew how powerful its industry was. He hoped a crushing first blow would buy Japan time.

shots.caption: Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto
Pearl Harbor and Battleship Row, December 1941

scenes.narration: The strike force left northern Japan in late November, keeping strict radio silence. It crossed the empty northern Pacific, far from normal shipping lanes. At its heart were six aircraft carriers under Vice Admiral Chuichi Nagumo: Akagi, Kaga, Soryu, Hiryu, Shokaku and Zuikaku. Between them they carried hundreds of aircraft.

shots.caption: The carrier Akagi in northern Japan before sailing
A Japanese Zero fighter on Akagi, December 1941

scenes.narration: There were warnings that morning. At about a quarter to four, a minesweeper spotted a periscope near the harbour entrance. At six thirty seven, the destroyer USS Ward fired on and sank a Japanese midget submarine. These were the first American shots of the Pacific war.

card.label: USS Ward sinks a midget submarine
card.note: The first American shots of the Pacific war

shots.caption: The destroyer USS Ward

scenes.narration: The Ward's report moved slowly up the chain of command. Then came the radar sighting at Opana. Privates Joseph Lockard and George Elliott kept tracking the planes as they came closer. They lost them near the coast, just before eight.

shots.caption: An SCR-270 radar antenna, the type used at Opana

card.label: Distance of the first radar sighting

scenes.narration: In Washington, Japanese diplomats had been told to deliver a long message at one o'clock in the afternoon, shortly before the attack. Delays in typing it up meant it arrived more than an hour after the bombs began to fall. American codebreakers had already read most of it.

shots.caption: Japanese envoys in Washington, December 1941

scenes.narration: The first wave hit airfields across Oahu just before eight. American planes, parked close together on the ground, were destroyed in rows. At Pearl Harbor itself, torpedo bombers swept in low over the water towards Battleship Row.

shots.file: File:Pearl Harbor- Nakajima B5N2 over Hickam- 80G178985.jpg
shots.caption: A Japanese bomber over Hickam Field
Torpedo tracks streak towards Battleship Row

scenes.narration: Leading the first wave was Commander Mitsuo Fuchida. As the attack began, he radioed back that surprise had been achieved. The code word was tora, the Japanese word for tiger, repeated three times. On the carriers, commanders now knew the Americans had been caught unprepared.

shots.file: File:Attack on Pearl Harbor Japanese planes view.jpg
shots.caption: Pearl Harbor seen from a Japanese aircraft

card.text: The signal that surprise had been achieved

shots.file: File:Pearl Harbor Japanese recon photo of battleship row 80G30551.jpg
shots.caption: Battleship Row, photographed from a Japanese plane

scenes.narration: Early in the attack, a bomb struck USS Arizona and set off her forward ammunition magazine. The battleship blew apart and sank within minutes. One thousand one hundred and seventy seven of her crew were killed, nearly half of all the Americans who died that day.

shots.file: File:The USS Arizona (BB-39) burning after the Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor - NARA 195617 - Edit.jpg
shots.caption: The wreck of USS Arizona after the attack

card.label: Men killed aboard USS Arizona
card.note: Nearly half of all US deaths that day

shots.file: File:USS SHAW exploding Pearl Harbor Nara 80-G-16871 2.jpg
shots.caption: The destroyer USS Shaw explodes, 7 December 1941

scenes.narration: Torpedoes tore into USS Oklahoma, which rolled over and capsized, trapping many of her crew. West Virginia and California also sank at their moorings. Black smoke from burning oil rose over the harbour, and sailors fought fires as the attack went on. Many fought back with whatever guns they could reach.

shots.caption: USS Oklahoma, capsized at her mooring

shots.query: USS West Virginia burning Pearl Harbor 1941
shots.caption: USS West Virginia burning after the attack

scenes.narration: On West Virginia, ship's cook Doris Miller helped carry wounded men, including the dying captain, to safety. Then, with no training, he manned an anti-aircraft machine gun until it ran out of ammunition. He became the first African American to receive the Navy Cross.

shots.caption: Doris Miller, ship's cook on USS West Virginia
Admiral Nimitz presents Miller with the Navy Cross, 1942

scenes.narration: A second wave of about one hundred and seventy planes followed within the hour. It struck the airfields and the harbour again. By mid-morning, the attackers had turned back to their carriers, leaving Pearl Harbor burning behind them.

shots.file: File:Akagi Pearl Harbor Second Wave Launch.jpg
shots.query: Akagi second wave launch Pearl Harbor
shots.caption: Planes take off from the carrier Akagi, 7 December 1941

shots.file: File:NARA 80-G-32915 Burned B-17 Flying Fortress on Hickam Field after Pearl Harbor attack.jpg
shots.caption: A burned-out B-17 bomber at Hickam Field

scenes.narration: In all, two thousand four hundred and three Americans were killed, sixty eight of them civilians. Another one thousand one hundred and seventy eight were wounded. Most of the dead were sailors, many of them trapped inside ships that sank.

Nineteen American ships were sunk or damaged, including eight battleships. One hundred and eighty eight aircraft were destroyed. Japan lost twenty nine planes and five midget submarines. One submarine crewman, Kazuo Sakamaki, was washed ashore and captured.

shots.file: File:Map showing ships present at Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941.png
shots.query: ships at Pearl Harbor 7 December 1941 map
shots.caption: Ships present at Pearl Harbor on 7 December

scenes.narration: Yet the attack missed what mattered most. The Pacific Fleet's three aircraft carriers were not in Pearl Harbor that morning. Within months, aircraft carriers, not battleships, would decide the war at sea. The Japanese had expected to find them there. Their absence was a stroke of luck for the Americans. Japan had struck the wrong ships.

shots.caption: USS Enterprise, one of the missing carriers

scenes.narration: The attackers also left the huge oil storage tanks, the repair yards and the submarine base almost untouched. Nagumo decided against launching a third strike. He judged that staying longer was too risky for his carriers. Yamamoto later called that decision a great mistake. Those fuel tanks and repair yards would help the fleet recover.

shots.caption: Fuel tanks at Pearl Harbor, left untouched

card.text: The fuel and the shipyards survived

scenes.narration: Most of the damaged battleships were raised and repaired. Six of the eight eventually returned to service, and some fought later in the war. Only Arizona and the old target ship Utah were never salvaged. They still lie in the harbour today.

shots.caption: Salvage work at Pearl Harbor, 1942
The wreck of Arizona in the 1950s

scenes.narration: The next day, President Franklin D. Roosevelt spoke to a joint session of Congress. He called the seventh of December a date which will live in infamy. Less than an hour later, Congress declared war on Japan.

shots.caption: Roosevelt addresses Congress, 8 December 1941

card.text: A date which will live in infamy

shots.caption: Roosevelt's draft, with 'infamy' written in by hand

scenes.narration: In the House of Representatives, the vote was three hundred and eighty eight to one. The only vote against came from Jeannette Rankin of Montana, a pacifist who had also voted against entering the First World War.

shots.caption: Representative Jeannette Rankin of Montana

card.label: House vote to declare war on Japan

shots.file: File:Franklin Roosevelt signing declaration of war against Japan.jpg
shots.query: Roosevelt signs declaration of war Japan
shots.caption: Roosevelt signs the declaration of war against Japan

scenes.narration: Three days later, on the eleventh of December, Germany and Italy declared war on the United States. The wars in Europe and the Pacific had become one global conflict. America's factories now turned to building ships, planes and tanks on an enormous scale. Japan, meanwhile, attacked British, American and Dutch territories across Asia.

card.text: Germany and Italy declare war on the US

scenes.narration: Many people believe that Yamamoto said Japan had only awakened a sleeping giant. That famous line comes from the 1970 film Tora! Tora! Tora!. There is no evidence that Yamamoto ever said or wrote it. The film's producers claimed it came from his diary, or from a letter. Neither has ever been found. The line was even reused in a 2001 Hollywood film.

shots.caption: Yamamoto aboard the battleship Nagato, 1940

scenes.narration: He did write something similar. In January 1942, in a letter to the Japanese politician Ogata Taketora, he warned that there was no glory in striking a sleeping enemy. He wrote that an angry enemy would soon strike back. Six months later, at the Battle of Midway, it did.

shots.query: Battle of Midway 1942 Japanese carrier burning
shots.caption: The Battle of Midway, June 1942

scenes.narration: Today, a white memorial stands over the sunken Arizona. It was dedicated in 1962. The bodies of most of her crew still lie inside the wreck. Small drops of oil still rise from her tanks to the surface, more than eighty years later.

shots.caption: The USS Arizona Memorial, built over the wreck
The USS Arizona Memorial today

card.text: Oil still rises from the Arizona

scenes.narration: Pearl Harbor was a stunning tactical success for Japan, but it failed in its main aim. It did not knock America out of the Pacific. It brought a united and determined United States into the war. Less than four years later, Japan surrendered. Sources and image credits are in the description.

shots.caption: The flag above the Arizona Memorial
